specPoints.text: know that an alloy is a mixture of a metal and one or more elements, usually other metals or carbon
explain why alloys are harder than pure metals

primer.text: From Extraction & Uses of Metals you have seen steel types doing jobs that pure iron cannot. This note explains why: alloys are mixtures whose different-sized atoms spoil the tidy atomic pattern of a pure metal, making the layers harder to slide. It also names brass, the classic copper-zinc alloy.

lessons.title: Alloys
lessons.opening: Alloys are mixtures: a metal combined with one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon. Steel, for example, is iron mixed with carbon. The blend often behaves very differently from the metals inside it: it can be stronger and harder, and it resists corrosion and extreme temperatures better. These enhanced properties are why alloys often beat pure metals in real uses.
keyPoints: Alloys are mixtures: either several metals together, or a metal with a non-metal such as carbon.
Steel is made from iron mixed with carbon.
Alloys are often stronger and harder than the metals they contain.
Many alloys resist corrosion or withstand extreme temperatures.
Brass, a common alloy, contains 70% copper and 30% zinc.

low.restatement: An alloy mixes a metal with other metals or with carbon, and the mixture often outperforms the original: harder, stronger, and better at resisting corrosion or heat. Brass, with copper and zinc, is the classic example.
low.analogy: Alloying is like blending two fruit juices: the result tastes different from either ingredient, and sometimes nicer.
low.examPointer: Definition questions want the mixture idea plus the examples: steel from iron and carbon, brass from copper and zinc.

medium.restatement: An alloy is a deliberate mixture of a metal with other elements, usually metals or carbon, chosen because the blend outperforms the pure metal. Steel shows the principle with iron and carbon, and brass with seventy percent copper and thirty percent zinc; the enhanced hardness, strength and corrosion resistance make alloys more useful than their ingredients.
medium.analogy: Think of a sports team: individual players are good, but the blended side, with different strengths on the pitch, wins more often than any line-up of identical players.
medium.examPointer: Diagram questions ask you to spot the alloy: choose the picture with unevenly sized particles and distorted rows.

check.stem: Which statement defines an alloy correctly?

options.text: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually metals or carbon
options.explanation: The mixture idea with metallic or carbon partners is the definition of record.

options.text: A pure metal refined until no impurities remain
options.explanation: That is the opposite of an alloy: alloying adds other elements on purpose.

options.text: A compound of a metal with oxygen
options.explanation: A compound is chemically bonded in a fixed ratio; an alloy is a mixture, and oxygen is not the usual partner.

options.text: Any metal extracted from an ore
options.explanation: Extraction produces the metal; alloying is a later, separate step of mixing.

check.stem: Steel is an alloy of which two substances?

options.text: Iron and carbon
options.explanation: The note gives steel as the example of a metal mixed with the non-metal carbon.

options.text: Copper and zinc
options.explanation: That pair makes brass, the other named alloy.

options.text: Iron and nickel only
options.explanation: Nickel appears in stainless steel, but steel in general is iron with carbon.

options.text: Iron and oxygen
options.explanation: Iron and oxygen make an oxide, which is a compound, not the steel mixture.

check.stem: What is the composition of brass?

options.text: 70% copper and 30% zinc
options.explanation: These are the exact figures the note quotes for brass.

options.text: 70% zinc and 30% copper
options.explanation: The shares are swapped; copper is the larger part of brass.

options.text: 70% iron and 30% carbon
options.explanation: That would be a very high-carbon steel, not brass.

options.text: 20% chromium and 10% nickel
options.explanation: Those are the stainless steel additions, not brass.

check.stem: Why are alloys often more useful than pure metals?

options.text: Their enhanced properties, such as being stronger, harder and more corrosion-resistant, fit demanding jobs
options.explanation: The mixture's properties can be very different from the ingredients, which is exactly what makes alloys useful.

options.text: They are always cheaper to extract from ores
options.explanation: Extraction applies to the metal, not the alloy; usefulness comes from the enhanced properties.

options.text: They are lighter than every pure metal
options.explanation: Weight is not the general claim; strength, hardness and resistance are.

options.text: They conduct electricity better than pure metals
options.explanation: Conductivity is not the listed enhancement; alloying usually harms conduction.

check.stem: Which pairing of alloy and ingredient set is correct?

options.text: Steel with iron and carbon; brass with copper and zinc
options.explanation: Both named alloys match their ingredients exactly as the note lists them.

options.text: Steel with copper and zinc; brass with iron and carbon
options.explanation: Both pairings are swapped between the two alloys.

options.text: Steel with copper and carbon; brass with iron and zinc
options.explanation: Neither pairing matches the note's compositions.

options.text: Steel with iron and zinc; brass with copper and carbon
options.explanation: The partners are crossed over incorrectly in both cases.

lessons.title: Why alloys are harder than pure metals
lessons.opening: Pure metals pack their atoms into neat, regular rows, and those rows slide easily over one another when a force is applied. Alloying spoils the pattern: atoms of different sizes distort the regular arrangement, so the layers can no longer slip smoothly. That is why alloys are harder than the pure metals they come from.
keyPoints: The atoms in an alloy come in different sizes.
The different sizes distort the regular arrangement of atoms in the metal.
Distorted layers make it more difficult for the atoms to slide over each other.
Layers that cannot slide easily make the alloy harder than the pure metal.
Diagram questions show the alloy as uneven particles sitting in distorted rows.

low.restatement: Different-sized atoms wreck the neat rows of a pure metal lattice, so the layers jam instead of sliding. Jammed layers mean a harder metal, which is the whole point of alloying.
low.analogy: It is like mixing pebbles of many sizes into a stack of identical marbles: the pile no longer rolls smoothly, and the shape holds firm.
low.examPointer: The explanation chain is examinable: different sizes, distorted arrangement, layers cannot slide, so the alloy is harder.

medium.restatement: In a pure metal the identical atoms form a regular lattice whose planes slip over one another under force, which is why pure metals are soft. Adding atoms of a different size distorts that lattice, so the planes no longer slide freely and the alloy holds its shape, appearing markedly harder than its parent metal.
medium.analogy: Picture a carpet that slides easily on a polished floor; scatter grit of mixed sizes under it and the carpet grips, exactly as foreign atoms grip the metal's planes.
medium.examPointer: Choose-the-diagram questions reward pattern spotting: uneven particle sizes with bent rows identify the alloy every time.

check.stem: Why are alloys harder than pure metals?

options.text: Different-sized atoms distort the layers, making them difficult to slide
options.explanation: The distorted, jammed layers are exactly why the alloy resists deformation and so feels harder.

options.text: Alloy atoms are larger, so the metal is more dense
options.explanation: Density is not the mechanism; the sliding of layers is.

options.text: Alloying forms strong new chemical bonds between metals
options.explanation: An alloy is a mixture, so no new compound or bond type is required for the hardness.

options.text: Alloys contain fewer free electrons, so they are stiffer
options.explanation: Electron count governs conduction, not hardness; the layer-sliding story is the answer.

check.stem: A question shows four particle diagrams. Which one represents an alloy?

options.text: Unevenly sized particles arranged in distorted rows
options.explanation: Mixed sizes and bent rows are the visual signature of the distorted alloy lattice.

options.text: Identical particles in perfectly straight rows
options.explanation: That is the pure metal, whose regular layers slide easily.

options.text: Identical particles in a jumbled gas-like spread
options.explanation: Alloys are solid lattices with distortion, not random spreads.

options.text: Paired particles joined by visible bonds
options.explanation: Molecules with bonds describe compounds, not the mixture structure of an alloy.

check.stem: Why are pure metals relatively soft?

options.text: Their identical atoms form regular layers that slide over each other easily
options.explanation: Smooth, regular planes slip under force, which is why pure metals deform readily.

options.text: Their atoms are too small to touch
options.explanation: Atoms in a metal are closely packed; softness comes from layer sliding.

options.text: They contain no electrons
options.explanation: Metals are full of delocalised electrons; this has nothing to do with softness.

options.text: Their layers are distorted by impurities
options.explanation: Distortion is the alloy story; pure metals have the undistorted layers.
options.misconception: alloy story applied to pure metals

check.stem: What effect does adding atoms of a different size have on the metal's structure?

options.text: It distorts the regular arrangement of the atoms
options.explanation: The foreign sizes push the neat rows out of line, which blocks easy sliding.

options.text: It makes the arrangement even more regular
options.explanation: Extra sizes do the opposite: they spoil the regularity.

options.text: It turns the metal into a compound
options.explanation: Mixing does not create a compound; the lattice simply becomes distorted.

options.text: It has no effect until the metal melts
options.explanation: The distortion exists in the solid and is present at everyday temperatures.

check.stem: Brass is harder than pure copper. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Zinc atoms of a different size distort copper's layers, so they cannot slide easily
options.explanation: Applying the general mechanism to brass: the zinc atoms jam the copper lattice's slip planes.

options.text: Zinc donates extra electrons that stiffen the copper
options.explanation: Electron donation is not the mechanism; distorted layers are.

options.text: Brass is a compound of copper and zinc with new bonds
options.explanation: Brass is a mixture; hardness comes from lattice distortion, not new bonding.

options.text: Copper's layers slide more easily when zinc is present
options.explanation: That would make brass softer, which contradicts the observation.

glossary.definition: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon.
The common alloy containing 70% copper and 30% zinc.
The gradual chemical attack on a metal, such as rusting, that alloys resist better than pure metals.
The regular, repeating arrangement of atoms in a solid metal.
The spoiling of the regular atomic arrangement caused by atoms of different sizes.

workedExample.prompt: a) Define an alloy and give the composition of one named example. b) Explain why brass is harder than pure copper. c) A particle diagram shows unevenly sized atoms sitting in distorted rows. What does it represent?
steps: a) An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon; brass contains 70% copper and 30% zinc.
b) In pure copper the atoms are all the same size in regular rows, so the layers slide over each other easily and the metal is soft.
In brass the different-sized zinc atoms distort the regular arrangement, so the layers can no longer slide easily — the alloy is harder.
c) It represents an alloy: uneven particle sizes with distorted layers are the alloy's signature in diagram questions.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) A mixture of a metal with other elements; brass = 70% Cu / 30% Zn. b) Different-sized atoms distort the layers and stop them sliding. c) An alloy.
